title: TTL mismatch eviction lattice postmortem and safeguard design
summary: Follow-up on a late-February KV cache eviction wave caused by TTL mismatch between application-side caching and Redwood prefix cache. Discussed RCA, short-term containment, and longer-term safeguards including canary policies, TTL harmonization, and telemetry improvements.
topics: Safeguard design: canaries, TTL contracts, fallback backoff
action_items: Alexei: share exact KV keyspace example and TTL mismatch diff (due 2026-03-18)
Martin Chu: push proposed canary rollout policy yaml to GitHub and link in ticket (due 2026-03-17)
Ivy Ramos: update runbook with containment script snippets and escalation path (due 2026-03-20)
Priya: deploy TTL harmonization patch to staging and report perf delta (due 2026-03-22)
next_steps: Redwood to provide a short benchmark of cache-hit improvement for TTL harmonization (Martin)
Customer to run staging canary with 10% traffic for 48 hrs and share observability dashboards (Alexei)
Schedule follow-up triage on 2026-03-24 to validate canary results (Sofia)
Ivy to circulate postmortem doc and collect signoffs from stakeholders
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-14 15:00 PDT — Duration: ~55 mins — Attendees: Sofia, Martin, Ivy — Alexei, Priya, Daniel, Lara

[00:00] Sofia (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick intro, this is a follow-up to the Feb 26th eviction wave, we wanted to run through the RCA and align on mitigations. I think Martin's got the excepts from the runtime traces.
[00:18] Martin (SE): yeah hi all — sorry for the ragged audio — um so quick TL;DR: we saw a sharp drop in KV cache hit-rate starting 02-26 02:14 UTC coincident with a deploy on your side, the runtime started evicting prefix entries much earlier than expected. That led to fallback amplification as many requests hit the backend model variants.
[00:37] Alexei (SRE): the timeline matches our deploy window, we also had autoscaler activity which added capacity but didn't stop the latency spike. We originally assumed this was just a spike in traffic but traces show eviction as the proximate cause.
[00:54] Priya (Backend): yeah, one thing — our service sets TTL in-application and we recently changed the default to 1m for some keys for faster freshness. I thought Redwood's prefix cache respects those headers but apparently there's a 5m default at the serving layer?
[01:11] Martin: exactly — we found mismatch between the app-set TTL and the serving-layer policy, the serving layer has a floor policy of 5m for shared prefix caches to reduce churn. when your app set 1m the runtime removed entries because it interpreted the shorter TTL, but because of the policy layering it created TTL churn across replicas, leading to oscillation.
[01:29] Daniel (Platform): hmm, that layering is subtle. Is this a config that we can override per-tenant? we didn't think it would be enforced like that.
[01:40] Martin: it's enforced to protect multi-tenant memory but we have per-account knobs, yes. in this case, the knob wasn't flipped. And there's a second factor: prefetch heuristics were disabled for that keyspace due to an opt-out label you had in prod, so cache warming didn't happen.
[02:02] Lara (PM): sorry to interrupt — so the root cause is both TTL drift and prefetch being off?
[02:08] Sofia: yes, TTL mismatch + opt-out prefetch + a timing of a small deploy + autoscaler scale-up, all together created a perfect storm. single factor alone likely wouldn't have caused the big impact.
[02:23] Alexei: we already rolled back the small deploy but the question is containment and how to avoid recurrences. we had 12 minutes of p95 latency doubling. that's customer-facing.
[02:33] Ivy (CSM): can you outline what you did immediately after the spike? for the record.
[02:38] Alexei: we forced the serving-layer TTL to 5m for the affected keyspace, re-enabled prefetch heuristics, and dialed the fallback backoff to avoid cascade. That brought hit-rate back up within ~7 minutes.
[02:50] Martin: logs show that after the forced change hit-rate recovered from 28% to about 78% within 6–8 minutes. but we lacked a canary: the change was broad and we risk regression.
[03:06] Priya: we were a bit panicked and ack'd the rollback. we need safer ways to test this.
[03:12] Martin: so immediate containment is fine but long-term fixes are multiple: 1) TTL contract — a small semantic contract between app and serving-layer so we don't have unexpected floor/ceiling disagreement; 2) canary policy for TTL and prefetch changes; 3) telemetry: add a delta alert when app-ttl vs runtime-ttl differs by more than X; 4) runbook updates.
[03:33] Sofia: let's unpack the TTL contract. Martin — what would that look like?
[03:36] Martin: propose: if app requests TTL T_app, the serving layer computes T_effective = clamp(T_app, tenant_min, tenant_max) and logs both values. tenant_min is per-account. default tenant_min currently is 5m. we should surface tenant_min in account settings and provide an override flag for critical keyspaces.
[03:52] Alexei: can we set tenant_min to 1m for our account? for certain keyspaces only?
[03:56] Martin: yes, per-keyspace override is feasible; we need a short validation window. we'd apply with a canary of 5–10% traffic for 24–48hrs.
[04:07] Daniel: about the prefetch opt-out — that was intentional for some ephemeral keys because we were worried about stale data. maybe we need to revisit that logic.
[04:16] Priya: could we have a hybrid prefetch? e.g., allow prefetch for hot keys and keep opt-out for cold ephemeral ones?
[04:22] Martin: that's reasonable — we can add a tag-based prefetch policy so opt-out only applies if label==cold. needs a little engineering.
[04:30] Lara: what's the risk if we do TTL harmonization without canaries? do we have rollback speed?
[04:36] Martin: the main risk is amplifying model cost and latency if we reduce tenant_min too low across hot keyspaces. rollback is a single API flip but you want monitoring in place for token-level cost spikes, latency, and hit-rate.
[04:49] Alexei: on monitoring — during the incident our dashboards didn't show the TTL delta metric, we only saw downstream latency. can we get a metric exposed in our Grafana?
[04:58] Martin: yes, we can emit app_ttl, runtime_ttl, and ttl_delta per key prefix to your metrics endpoint. we'll add an alert rule: if ttl_delta > 120s for >5 min and hit-rate < 50% then page SRE on-call.
[05:14] Priya: could be noisy if we set threshold too low. maybe threshold should be relative to baseline hit-rate.
[05:20] Martin: agreed, we'll make it composite: ttl_delta condition AND hit-rate drop condition.
[05:25] Sofia: ok let's capture short-term vs long-term. Short-term: tenant_min override for affected keyspace, enable prefetch for hot keys, add ttl_delta metric and composite alert, and publish runbook. Long-term: TTL contract, per-keyspace canary framework, telemetry enrichment, and UI to show tenant_min.
[05:44] Ivy: for the runbook can we include exact steps you took? Alexei already documented some but a combined doc would help.
[05:50] Alexei: yes, I have the containment commands and times, will paste into the postmortem doc.
[05:54] Martin: i'll draft the canary YAML and the monitoring changes in a repo branch.
[05:58] Sofia: great. any open questions from customer side?
[06:02] Priya: what about cost — if we reduce tenant_min for our account there is potential token cost increase because more hot entries may be cached shorter and cause churn?
[06:12] Martin: token cost impact depends on your access patterns. we'll run a simple sim for your recent 7-day trace and estimate incremental tokens. we'll attach that to the canary PR.
[06:22] Lara: and compliance/audit — we need to ensure changes are logged for SOC2/ISO when we adjust tenant configs.
[06:30] Ivy: Redwood can provide audit logs for tenant config flips, we keep KMS logs as well. we'll add a ticket to ensure compliance capturing.
[06:38] Daniel: suggestion — add a tolerance header so app can say 'best-effort-ttl: true' to indicate it's ok if runtime clamps, that would reduce alerts.
[06:47] Martin: interesting, yes we can consider a BEST_EFFORT flag. needs product discussion.
[06:51] Sofia: ok, we're at 25 minutes in the meeting transcript here — i'll skip forward and summarize the rest: we assigned tasks, agreed on canary cadence, and documented monitoring thresholds.
[07:05] [skipping to Q&A] Alexei: how quickly can you get the ttl_delta metric flowing?
[07:09] Martin: i can have a basic metric pipeline in 48 hours, prod emit in 72–96 hours depending on approvals.
[07:15] Priya: can we get a temporary dashboard template to copy?
[07:18] Martin: yes, i'll push a Grafana json and a sample alert rule.
[07:22] Sofia: any blockers for the canary? customer has to flip per-keyspace override and Redwood to push canary config.
[07:29] Alexei: we'll prepare the keyspace list and sample keys by 03-18.
[07:33] Martin: ok we'll do a 10% traffic canary for 48 hrs, monitor hit-rate, latency p95 and token cost. if all good — ramp to 50% then full.
[07:43] Ivy: schedule follow-up on 03-24 to review canary outcomes.
[07:46] Sofia: perfect. quick recap: action items and owner assignment, and we will circulate the postmortem doc. thanks everyone.
[07:55] [00:00:00. start-of-file footer noise]
notes: Customer had partial observability gap around TTL vs runtime TTL
Containment was effective but lacked canary safety
Telemetry and runbook improvements are highest priority
